lesson.title: Where Are the Crypto Millionaires Who Lost Everything? Survivorship Bias
lesson.summary: Survivorship bias is the error of drawing conclusions from the visible survivors of a process while ignoring the failures that never make it into view, and crypto success stories are a near perfect illustration of the trap.
lesson.body:
Survivorship bias is the error of concentrating attention on the people, projects, or objects that survived a selection process while overlooking those that did not survive, even though the failures often carry the more important information. The clearest illustration comes from statistician Abraham Wald's work for the military during the Second World War. Researchers examined returning aircraft and found bullet holes concentrated on the wings and fuselage, and the initial instinct was to add armor exactly where the damage was visible. Wald pointed out the flaw: the planes being examined were the ones that survived their damage. The planes hit in the areas with no bullet holes on the survivors, such as the engines, were the ones that never made it back, so those were the areas that actually needed reinforcing.

The bias persists because failure is systematically less visible than success. A person who made a fortune trading a particular cryptocurrency has every incentive to talk about it publicly, while a person who lost their savings on a similar bet quietly stops posting, deletes the relevant social media history, or simply never had a platform to begin with. Failed projects get delisted from exchanges, abandon their websites, and vanish from search results, while successful projects remain visible indefinitely, which means the sample of outcomes any observer actually sees is skewed toward success well before any conscious evaluation begins.

Crypto investment folklore runs almost entirely on survivorship bias. The story of an early adopter who bought Bitcoin for a few dollars and became a millionaire circulates widely, and it is used, explicitly or implicitly, to argue that buying and holding cryptocurrency is a reliable path to wealth. That argument only works by looking exclusively at Bitcoin, which is one of thousands of cryptocurrencies launched since 2009, and ignoring the large majority of coins and tokens from the same era that lost most or all of their value, were abandoned by their developers, or turned out to be outright fraud. The visible millionaire is real, but the sample used to generalize from that outcome, all cryptocurrencies ever launched, is not the sample being examined, only the survivors are.

The same distortion applies to trading advice and influencer track records. An account that made several correct calls in a row and gained a large following looks like evidence of skill, but that visibility is itself a product of survivorship: among a large population of people making similar bets, some will get a lucky streak purely by chance, and those are precisely the accounts likely to gain followers and stay active, while the far larger number who guessed wrong quietly go silent. Without knowing the full population of people who made similar predictions, and how many of them were wrong, a string of visible correct calls provides much weaker evidence of skill than it appears to.

Correcting for survivorship bias means deliberately asking about the failures that are not on display: how many similar projects launched in the same period, and what happened to them, not just the one or two that are still visible and being discussed. It also means being suspicious of any argument built entirely from named success stories rather than from a defined population and its full range of outcomes. This bias reinforces the availability heuristic, covered next, because the visible survivors are also the examples that come to mind most easily, compounding the distortion rather than counteracting it.
